summary: Discusses multi-endpoint topologies in RTP environments, mapping centralized video conferencing setups to RTP terminology. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 7667.

plainLanguage.summary: This draws pictures of the different ways many people can connect in a video call, with a central box or directly, and names them. It was replaced by RFC 7667.

questions: video conferencing mixers and translators in rtp
subtitle: How many people connect in RTP video calls: direct, through a mixer, or via a switching device.

tldr.problem: RTP (the protocol for video and audio calls) was designed for two people talking, but real deployments need many people in one call. The standard did not clearly define how multi-endpoint topologies should work.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5117 maps common video conferencing setups to RTP terminology. It defines how devices called Mixers and Translators can be used to connect multiple endpoints, explains different ways they handle media and control information, and clarifies RTCP (control protocol) behavior in each case.
tldr.outcome: Provides clarity for implementers of video conferencing systems. The RFC was later updated by RFC 7667 with more detailed analysis and recommendations.

today: RFC 5117 is an Informational RFC from January 2008. It was superseded by RFC 7667 in November 2015, which provides more detailed analysis, recommendations for modern use cases, and guidance for multimedia congestion control in multipoint scenarios. Both RFCs remain references for video conferencing system design.

sections.title: Topology Overview
sections.content:
RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) is the standard for sending audio and video over networks. RFC 3550 defined RTP primarily for point-to-point calls (two people), but modern deployments require multi-endpoint scenarios with many participants on one call.

The problem: implementations use devices called Multipoint Control Units (MCUs) to manage group calls, but the term "MCU" is vague and implementations vary widely. Different manufacturers implement the same box differently. To standardize on how RTP should work with multiple endpoints, RFC 5117 maps common video conferencing topologies (the shapes of how devices connect) to RTP's defined concepts.

This document is not a standard—it is explanatory. It clarifies how the Mixers and Translators described in RFC 3550 should work in real deployments.
sections.plainLanguage: Video calls started with two people. Now many people join one call. The RFC explains what MCUs (video boxes) should do and how they talk to each other using RTP.

sections.title: Basic Topologies
sections.content:
Point-to-Point (Topo-Point-to-Point) is the simplest: two endpoints connect directly, both sending and receiving. RTCP (control information) goes directly between them. No complexity arises from multiple sources.

Multicast (Topo-Multicast) uses IP multicast: all endpoints send to a shared multicast address and receive from it. All participants see all streams and all control messages. This works well in networks with multicast support but requires feedback suppression to avoid overwhelming the network with control messages.

Translator (Topo-Translator) is a relay box. Transport Translators bridge different network domains (for example, multicast on one side, unicast on the other) without changing media. Media Translators also convert the audio or video format. A Translator forwards each incoming stream as an individual outgoing stream, keeping the stream identity (SSRC, in RTP terms) the same across the translation.
sections.plainLanguage: Point-to-Point is two people. Multicast is everyone shouting and everyone listening. A Translator is a repeater that forwards calls between networks.

sections.title: Mixer and MCU Models
sections.content:
Mixer (Topo-Mixer) is fundamentally different from a Translator. A Mixer receives multiple streams, combines (mixes) them together, and sends out a new stream under its own identity (SSRC). The original sources are identified in the CSRC (Contributing Source) field of the output stream. A Mixer processes RTCP reports from all inputs and generates its own reports. Each participant receives a mixed view suitable to their network bandwidth.

Video Switching MCU (Topo-Video-switch-MCU) forwards a single selected stream at a time instead of mixing. It chooses based on voice activity (who is talking), floor control, or presentation mode. It may transcode the stream to adapt to the recipient's network. The main drawback: participants not shown hear nothing, confusing congestion control and quality reporting.

RTCP-Terminating MCU (Topo-RTCP-terminating-MCU) runs separate RTP sessions with each participant (not a shared session). This means each connection is independent. The MCU may mix content or select streams. However, it breaks the RTP session continuity: participants do not see who contributed to the content (CSRC information is lost). This can cause problems with loop detection and speaker identification.
sections.plainLanguage: A Mixer blends all the audio/video together and sends one combined stream. A Switching MCU picks one person's stream and sends it. An RTCP-Terminating MCU runs separate calls with each person but the MCU handles talking to them all.

sections.title: RTCP and Control Information
sections.content:
The biggest differences between topologies appear in how they handle RTCP (the control protocol). In point-to-point and multicast, RTCP messages flow directly. In a Translator, RTCP is forwarded, but media Translators must rewrite RTCP fields to account for format changes.

A Mixer must not forward RTCP unchanged. Instead, it generates its own receiver reports (saying what it received) for each domain it serves. Senders in other domains have no direct view of each other's reception quality; they only see the Mixer's reports.

A Video Switching MCU that forwards only one stream causes issues: participants sending content that is not selected see no receiver reports for their media, making them think the network has failed. This is why RFC 5117 recommends implementing Mixer behavior instead.

An RTCP-Terminating MCU terminates all RTCP flows at the MCU. Again, it breaks the shared RTP session: endpoints cannot reliably determine who contributed to the content being shown. Signaling protocols (like SIP conference packages) must compensate by identifying speakers outside of RTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Control messages (RTCP) are the tricky part. Mixers change them to report on the mixed stream. Switching MCUs can confuse senders about reception. Terminating MCUs split the session, losing RTP-level speaker info.

sections.title: Comparing and Combining Topologies
sections.content:
The key topology properties are: whether all endpoints see all media, whether media interoperability (format conversion) is needed, whether bit-rate adaptation per receiver is supported, whether media is aggregated, whether all participants are visible in RTP headers, and whether loop detection is possible.

Point-to-Point offers simplicity but does not scale. Multicast scales but requires multicast infrastructure. Translators are simple but do not aggregate. Mixers aggregate and adapt to each receiver but require media processing. Video Switching MCUs are simple but lose quality information. RTCP-Terminating MCUs are widely deployed but break RTP session continuity.

Complex deployments may combine topologies: for instance, Mixers or Translators can connect to each other. However, this requires careful SSRC/CSRC management. The key rule: the SSRC space must be shared across all Mixers and Translators in a connected conference to allow loop detection (detecting when audio/video accidentally feeds back to itself).
sections.plainLanguage: Each topology has trade-offs: simplicity, scalability, media quality, visibility. Complex conferences chain them together but must keep track of sources to avoid loops.
